extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, graduate students, and critics working in narratology and novel studies (esp. readers of Genette and Proust)
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and classifying the temporal devices and relations in a novel's discourse (duration, pauses/description, ellipses, scenes, frequency) and assessing their function in pacing, characterization, and narrative coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration
rubrics_metrics.description: The way narrative time is stretched or compressed — changes of tempo in the text (accelerations, summaries, implied silences) that make time appear in the guise of years or decades rather than successive quarters of an hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for sudden tempo changes that are not prepared by preceding lines ("extraordinary change of tempo"), chapter breaks or ellipses that create an impression of long duration, and narrative devices of acceleration (Genette cites Proust's own phrase about novelists being "obliged, by wildly accelerating the beat of the pendulum, to transport the reader...over ten, or twenty, or even thirty years"). Compare treatments (e.g., Proust's wild accelerations vs. Balzacian summaries). Note whether tempo change is signaled or implied, and whether it produces a felt 'silence' or lift-off for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive pauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional 'descriptive pauses' are portions of description thought to slow or suspend narrative action; Genette examines their number, length, and formal type (many Proustian descriptions are relatively few, short, or iterative and thus do not create pauses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether descriptive passages function as true narrative pauses (suspending action) or are integrated into narrative time. Count and measure descriptions (Genette notes ~30 clear descriptive passages in Proust, most under four pages) and identify iterative descriptions (synthesizing several occurrences into one section) which typically do not slow the narrative. Contrast with Balzac's extratemporal descriptive canon (descriptions given by the narrator 'for the reader') and with writers who integrate description into character action or gaze (Stendhal, Flaubert). Beware the anti-pattern of treating all description as a simple temporal pause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proustian description as perceptual narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: In Proust, 'description' often functions not as object-reporting but as a narrative of the character's perceptual activity — impressions, progressive discoveries, shifts in perspective, errors and corrections — and thus contains 'a whole story' rather than constituting a pause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating description, determine if it is principally an account of a character's active perception (e.g., Elstir's seascapes, Aunt Leonie's lime-blossoms, Hubert Robert's fountain). Such description is dialogical/psychological and temporal (it occupies time in the diegesis), so it should be treated as scene-like narrative rather than an extratemporal ecphrasis. Identify markers in the language (verbs and locutions like 'seem', 'appear', 'gave the impression', 'you thought', etc.) that foreground perceptual process over static depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis (temporal): types and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal ellipses are omissions of story-time; they may be definite (duration indicated) or indefinite (not indicated), and formally explicit (text signals the lapse) or implicit/hypothetical (inferred by the reader or only revealed later). Genette also distinguishes 'characterizing' ellipses (which provide diegetic content about the elided period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify ellipses you find as: (a) explicit (with time indication or later time marker), which can function like quick summaries or iconic representations of void; (b) implicit (reader must infer gaps from chronological lacunae); (c) hypothetical (no clear localisation, revealed only by subsequent analepses). Note whether ellipses are characterized (e.g., 'some years of happiness passed'), whether they provide diegetic content retrospectively, and how they affect hermeneutics (some ellipses remain opaque and significant, e.g., the mute months after the grandmother's death). Consider how ellipses limit or challenge precise temporal analysis of the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene — role and transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene (in the temporal sense) is redefined in Proust: scene becomes dominant in the text, but its function changes from being primarily dramatic to often paradigmatic, illustrative, or inauguratory (entries into milieus that stand for a series), and scenes are frequently 'inflated' with digressions, retrospections, anticipations, iteratives, and narratorly interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than assuming scenes equate to high dramatic action, evaluate whether scenes operate as paradigmatic inaugural moments (e.g., Guermantes matinees, dinners, soirees) that represent a whole series of similar events. Measure the proportion of strictly narrative/dramatic content vs. discursive/descriptive/digressive material within scenes (Genette gives sample proportions for Proust's large scenes). Identify whether a scene functions as a 'temporal hearth' gathering diverse information, and whether its inflation with parenthetical material transforms its temporal texture away from classical 'scenic' temporality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative frequency (singulative vs. iterative relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequency concerns relations of repetition between narrated events (diegesis) and narrative statements (text). Four virtual types arise from whether events and statements are singular or repeated (e.g., narrating once what happened once = 'singulative'; narrating n times what happened n times corresponds iconically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify occurrences according to whether the narrative statement's multiplicity matches the event's multiplicity: 1) narrating once what happened once (singulative/singular scene); 2) narrating n times what happened n times (anaphoric, still singulative in Genette's technical sense because number matches). Be prepared to locate and label the other two relations (n times what happened once; once what happened n times) in further analysis. Note that 'repetition' is an abstraction — identify whether 'identity' is invoked by the narrative or constructed by the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative descriptions (synthesizing repeated occurrences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions that are not tied to a unique diegetic moment but synthesize several analogous occurrences into a single descriptive section (iterative type), and therefore do not function to slow narrative; they often compress repeated experiences into a unified portrayal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify iterative descriptions (Genette cites Leonie's room, the church at Combray, 'views of the sea', hotels, scenery of Venice) and treat them as compressive/schematic devices rather than temporal pauses. Quantify their presence (Genette estimates more than a third of clear descriptions are iterative) and assess their narrative effect: they usually accelerate or generalize rather than suspend the story. Distinguish iterative description from single-instance description connected to a character's contemplative halt.
